title: Landlord Entity Change and Unexecuted SNDA at Lease Renewal
scenario:
**Yardi Voyager — Property: 200 Parkview Plaza, Suite 400**
Tenant: DataSync Corp | Lease ID: PV-2019-0412 | Landlord Entity: Parkview Office Partners LLC | Term: 7 yrs commencing 4/1/2019 | NNN w/ CPI escalator | Base rent: $42.50/SF | Renewal option: 5-yr at 95% FMV

**Shared Drive — \\ntserver\properties\parkview\acquisitions\**
File: 'NovaTerra_Parkview_Acquisition_Closing_Memo.pdf' (dated 9/15/2024)
Purchaser: NovaTerra Parkview Holdings LLC | Seller: Parkview Office Partners LLC | All tenant leases assigned per Section 14 of PSA | SNDA delivery required within 90 days of closing per buyer's lender.

**DocuSign — Envelope: SNDA-PV-2024-batch**
Status: Sent (10/2/2024) | Recipients: 14 tenants | DataSync Corp (Suite 400): Status = 'Declined' (10/18/2024) | Reason noted by signer: 'Counsel advises we cannot execute without landlord confirming TI reimbursement obligation transfers.'

**Outlook — From: j.morrison@novaterra.com To: c.brennan@novaterra.com (11/4/2024)**
'Catherine — DataSync never signed the SNDA. Their counsel is being difficult about the TI carryover. I spoke with Marcus at lunch and he said just proceed without it for now, the assignment clause in the PSA covers us. Let's circle back after year-end.'

**MRI Software (acquired portfolio) — Tenant Ledger Cross-Ref**
Note: DataSync Corp also appears as tenant at Meridian Tower (acquired portfolio), Suite 1200, under lease MER-2021-0087 with landlord entity 'Greystone Capital Realty LLC' (pre-acquisition name). That SNDA WAS executed post-acquisition.

**Outlook — From: DataSync legal (forwarded chain, 2/3/2025)**
> Original from DataSync counsel → NovaTerra legal:
> 'Per our earlier correspondence, DataSync intends to exercise its renewal option at Parkview. However, we note the SNDA remains unexecuted. Our position is that renewal notice must be delivered to the original landlord entity (Parkview Office Partners LLC) as named in the lease, since no attornment has been established with NovaTerra Parkview Holdings LLC.'

**Teams — #parkview-leasing (2/5/2025, 3:47 PM)**
@c.brennan: Has anyone dealt with a renewal notice addressed to a dissolved entity?
@m.santos: Parkview Office Partners wasn't dissolved, it was just the seller. Check the PSA assignment language.
@c.brennan: Right but the tenant is saying without the SNDA they don't recognize us as landlord
@m.santos: (thumbs_up emoji, no further reply)
question: DataSync Corp has sent renewal notice addressed to 'Parkview Office Partners LLC.' Given the unexecuted SNDA, the PSA assignment clause, and the tenant's position, what is the correct administrative determination regarding the validity of this renewal notice?
choices: A) The renewal notice is invalid because it was not delivered to the current landlord entity (NovaTerra Parkview Holdings LLC); DataSync must re-deliver to the correct entity within the option exercise window.

B) The renewal notice is valid; the PSA assignment transferred all landlord rights and obligations regardless of the unexecuted SNDA, and the tenant's delivery to the original named entity constitutes constructive notice to the successor.
C) The renewal notice is invalid because the unexecuted SNDA means no attornment relationship exists; NovaTerra has no standing as landlord until the SNDA is executed.
D) The renewal cannot be processed until both the SNDA and TI reimbursement transfer are resolved; the notice should be held in abeyance pending legal resolution.
rationale: The PSA explicitly assigned all tenant leases to NovaTerra Parkview Holdings LLC. An SNDA (Subordination, Non-Disturbance, and Attornment Agreement) is primarily for the lender's benefit and to protect the tenant in foreclosure scenarios — its absence does not negate the assignment of the landlord's interest under the purchase and sale agreement. The lease's own Section 14 (referenced in the PSA closing memo) governs assignment. DataSync's renewal notice, while addressed to the former entity name, constitutes valid exercise of their option because NovaTerra is the legal successor and the notice demonstrates clear intent to renew. Answer A is wrong because it would penalize the tenant for using the entity name in their lease when the landlord failed to complete the SNDA process. Answer C conflates the SNDA's purpose (lender protection/foreclosure attornment) with the basic landlord-tenant succession that occurs via PSA assignment. Answer D represents an overly conservative approach that would risk the renewal window expiring, potentially exposing NovaTerra to a claim that they frustrated the tenant's contractual renewal right.

title: COVID Base Year CAM Reconciliation Dispute with Gross-Up Ambiguity
scenario:
**Yardi Voyager — CAM Reconciliation Worksheet: Lakeshore Commons, 2024 Actuals**
Tenant: Vertex Consulting Group | Suite 300 | Pro-rata share: 8.7% | Base year: 2020 | Expense stop: $12.85/SF (2020 actual) | 2024 actual operating expenses: $18.42/SF | Tenant's estimated overage billed: $4.20/SF | Actual overage: $5.57/SF | Variance due: $1.37/SF = $38,356

**Shared Drive — \\ntserver\leases\lakeshore\vertex\**
File: 'Vertex_Lease_Executed_2020-01-15.pdf'
Section 7.2: 'Tenant's share of Operating Expenses in excess of Base Year Operating Expenses...'
Section 7.4: 'Base Year shall mean calendar year 2020 actual Operating Expenses.'
Section 7.6: 'Operating Expenses shall be adjusted to reflect at least 95% occupancy during any year in which the Building is less than 95% occupied.' [Note: this gross-up clause applies to COMPARISON years only — no equivalent language for Base Year adjustment]

**MRI Software — Legacy Portfolio Note (imported record)**
Property: Lakeshore Commons | 2020 occupancy: 41% (COVID impact) | 2020 operating expenses as-incurred: $12.85/SF | 2020 expenses if grossed-up to 95%: $17.10/SF | Note added by former SVP R. Hartley (departed 3/2025): 'COVID base year issue — flag for reconciliation disputes starting 2023. Multiple tenants affected.'

**Outlook — From: vertex.counsel@kirklandshaw.com To: c.brennan@novaterra.com (1/22/2025)**
'Ms. Brennan — Our client disputes the 2024 CAM reconciliation. The 2020 base year reflects artificially depressed expenses due to the pandemic shutdown. Building occupancy was 41%. Had the building been at normal occupancy, expenses would have been materially higher, resulting in a higher expense stop. We believe equitable adjustment is warranted and request the base year be grossed-up to 95% occupancy consistent with Section 7.6 methodology.'

**Outlook — From: r.hartley@novaterra.com To: leasing-team@novaterra.com (6/12/2023, archived)**
'Team — heads up. We're going to start seeing base year disputes on 2020-vintage leases at Lakeshore. I reviewed the Vertex lease specifically. Section 7.6 gross-up only applies to comparison years, NOT the base year. This was intentional — we negotiated it that way because we wanted a low base year to maximize recoveries. DO NOT concede grossing up the base year. The lease is clear.'
[This email is in R. Hartley's archived mailbox — requires legal hold access]

**Teams — #cam-reconciliation (1/28/2025, 11:15 AM)**
@c.brennan: Anyone remember the rationale on the Lakeshore 2020 base year gross-up question? Vertex counsel is pushing hard.
@j.patel: I think Hartley had a view on this before he left. Check his files?
@c.brennan: His mailbox is archived. Would need legal hold request.
@j.patel: Maybe just check the lease language? Section 7.6 seems pretty clear to me that gross-up applies generally
@c.brennan: That's what Vertex is arguing too (thinking_face emoji)
question: Based on the lease language, the archived institutional knowledge, and the tenant's counsel's argument, what is the correct position for NovaTerra on the Vertex 2024 CAM reconciliation dispute?
choices: A) The dispute should be split — apply a partial gross-up to the base year using actual 2020 occupancy (41%) as a compromise, resulting in an adjusted stop of approximately $14.90/SF.
B) Vertex's position is correct; Section 7.6 gross-up methodology should be applied to the base year, adjusting the expense stop to $17.10/SF, reducing the tenant's 2024 overage to $1.32/SF.
C) The reconciliation cannot be finalized until R. Hartley's archived emails are retrieved via legal hold to confirm the original negotiation intent; the matter should be tabled pending that review.

D) NovaTerra should maintain that the base year is $12.85/SF as stated in the lease; Section 7.6 gross-up applies only to comparison years, not the base year, and the 2024 overage of $5.57/SF stands as calculated.
rationale: The lease language is dispositive here. Section 7.6 explicitly provides for gross-up adjustment to reflect 95% occupancy, but this clause governs Operating Expenses in comparison years. Section 7.4 defines the Base Year as '2020 actual Operating Expenses' with no gross-up provision. The absence of gross-up language for the base year, combined with its explicit inclusion for comparison years, demonstrates intentional drafting — if the parties intended gross-up for both, they would have said so. Hartley's archived email confirms this was a deliberate negotiation strategy, but the lease language alone supports the position without needing that email. Answer A incorrectly applies Section 7.6 to the base year when the lease limits it to comparison years. Answer C invents a compromise with no contractual basis — commercial lease disputes are resolved by contract language, not equitable splitting. Answer D is unnecessarily conservative; while Hartley's email provides helpful context, the lease language is unambiguous and NovaTerra need not delay its position pending retrieval of supporting correspondence.

title: Sublease Consent and Related-Entity Principal Identification Across Systems
scenario:
**Yardi Voyager — Lease Record: Tribune Tower, Suite 1800**
Tenant: Orion Strategic Advisors LLC | Lease ID: TT-2021-0033 | Term: 10 yrs | Commencement: 7/1/2021 | Base rent: $55.00/SF | 12,400 SF | NNN | Sublease clause: Section 22.1 — 'Tenant shall not sublease without Landlord's prior written consent, which shall not be unreasonably withheld. Landlord may consider financial condition of proposed subtenant.'

**DocuSign — Envelope: Sublease-Consent-TT-1800 (completed 8/14/2024)**
Sublessor: Orion Strategic Advisors LLC | Proposed Subtenant: Polaris Capital Partners LLC | Space: 4,200 SF of Suite 1800 | Term: 3 years | Approved by: Marcus Webb, SVP Leasing (signature on file) | Financial review attachment: Polaris Capital Partners LLC — D&B rating: 3A2, annual revenue $8.2M

**Salesforce — Contact Record**
Name: Daniel Koh | Company: Orion Strategic Advisors LLC | Title: Managing Partner | Also linked to: Account 'Polaris Capital Partners LLC' (role: 'Board Advisor')

**Shared Drive — \\ntserver\leases\tribune\1800\sublease\**
File: 'Polaris_Subtenant_Application.pdf'
Principal listed: James Aldrich, Managing Director | Guarantor: None requested
File: 'IL_SOS_Polaris_Filing.pdf'
Illinois Secretary of State filing: Polaris Capital Partners LLC | Registered Agent: Daniel Koh | Members: Daniel Koh (60%), James Aldrich (40%) | Formation date: 3/12/2024

**Outlook — From: m.webb@novaterra.com To: c.brennan@novaterra.com (8/10/2024)**
'Catherine — Polaris financials look fine. D&B is acceptable. Go ahead and route the consent for my signature. Quick turnaround please, Orion's been waiting.'

**Outlook — From: m.webb@novaterra.com To: personal archive (draft, never sent, 8/9/2024)**
'Note to self — Polaris Capital. Daniel Koh is listed as registered agent. He's the same Koh who runs Orion. Essentially subleasing to himself? Lease doesn't explicitly prohibit but feels like it should have been flagged. Orion's been a good tenant though. Let it go.'
[This draft was recovered during M. Webb's departure transition in 1/2025]

**Building Engines — Maintenance Request (11/3/2024)**
Requester: Daniel Koh | Suite: 1800 | Company listed: 'Orion/Polaris' | Request: 'Need after-hours HVAC for the Polaris side — same access card as my Orion credentials please.'

**Teams — #tribune-tower-ops (1/15/2025, 2:22 PM)**
@facilities.mgr: Quick Q — Suite 1800 subtenant (Polaris) keeps using Orion's access credentials and parking allocation. Are they actually separate companies?
@c.brennan: Technically yes per the sublease docs. Why?
@facilities.mgr: Same guy (Dan Koh) badges in for both. Just want to make sure we're billing correctly.
@c.brennan: (eyes emoji) Let me look into this.
question: Given the evidence across all systems, what is the most significant lease administration issue that Catherine Brennan should escalate regarding the Polaris sublease?
choices: A) The sublease consent was granted based on an incomplete financial review — Polaris was formed only 5 months before the sublease application, making the D&B rating unreliable, and no personal guaranty was obtained for a newly-formed entity controlled by the primary tenant's principal.

B) The sublease is unauthorized because Section 22.1 requires that the subtenant be a genuinely independent third party; a related entity controlled by the same principal constitutes a de facto assignment requiring different consent standards.

C) There is no material issue — the sublease consent was properly obtained per Section 22.1, the subtenant's financials met the threshold, and common ownership between tenant and subtenant is not prohibited by the lease.
D) The sublease consent is voidable because Marcus Webb failed to disclose a conflict of interest when approving it; his unsent draft shows he identified the related-party issue but suppressed it.
rationale: The core issue is risk exposure from an inadequate financial review. Polaris Capital Partners LLC was formed in March 2024 — just five months before the sublease consent was executed. A D&B rating for a 5-month-old entity is essentially meaningless; it reflects no operating history. The subtenant application listed James Aldrich as principal (obscuring Koh's majority ownership), and no guaranty was requested despite the entity's newness. This matters because if Polaris defaults, NovaTerra's recourse is limited to an entity with no track record and no guarantor. The related-party aspect (Koh controlling both entities) amplifies the risk: if Orion experiences financial difficulty, Polaris likely will too, and the sublease rent stream that Orion depends on to offset its own obligation becomes unreliable. Answer D overstates Webb's obligation — his draft note shows awareness but not a 'conflict of interest' in the legal sense; he had no personal financial interest. Answer C misreads Section 22.1 — most commercial leases do not prohibit related-entity subleases, and the clause says consent shall not be 'unreasonably withheld,' which courts interpret narrowly. Answer D ignores that 'not unreasonably withheld' still permits landlord to consider financial condition, and the financial review was materially deficient given Polaris's formation date.
